Document Title: Scalable Rigidity Maintenance Strategies for Networked Multirobot Systems: Overcoming Decentralized Coordination Challenges
Authors: J. Francisco Presenza; E. Pecker‐Marcosig; I. Mas; J. Ignacio Alvarez‐Hamelin; J. I. Giribet
Author Affiliations: Facultad de Ingeniería, Universidad de Buenos Aires, Ciudad Autónoma de Buenos Aires, Argentina; Facultad de Ingeniería, Universidad de Buenos Aires, Ciudad Autónoma de Buenos Aires, Argentina; Universidad de San Andrés and CONICET, Victoria, Buenos Aires, Argentina; Facultad de Ingeniería, Universidad de Buenos Aires, Ciudad Autónoma de Buenos Aires, Argentina; Universidad de San Andrés and CONICET, Victoria, Buenos Aires, Argentina
Publication Title: Resilient Complex Adaptive Systems: Modeling, Simulation, Visualization and Engineering Approaches
Abstract: Multirobot systems (MRSs)—an active area of research in recent decades—can be viewed as a subclass of resilient complex adaptive systems (CASs), where each robot functions as an autonomous agent in a bottom‐up architecture. Fundamental challenges arise when only relative information is available. This chapter addresses the control and localization of multirobot networks in which agents rely solely on relative distance measurements to their neighbors. Since sensing and communication ranges are limited, the network experiences changes in its topology as robots move. This can result in the loss of rigidity—the structural condition that allows position estimation through distance measurements—thereby causing the control schemes to fail. Different approaches to rigidity maintenance in networks with dynamic topologies are discussed, highlighting their respective advantages and limitations in terms of scalability and communication requirements. To illustrate the use of the proposed approach, a distributed control law is presented, where each agent exchanges local information with its near neighbors to achieve collaborative objectives. This decentralized, interaction‐driven adaptation exemplifies CAS principles, with global resilience emerging from local behaviors. Through the exploration of rigidity maintenance in networked systems, this chapter offers insights and methodologies that promise to advance the state‐of‐the‐art in resilient MRSs design and deployment.
